title: Hydrodynamic description of correlation matrix eigenvalues in a finite temperature expanding free fermionic gas
authors: Atharva Naik, Madhumita Saha, David A. Huse, Manas Kulkarni, Abhishek Dhar
abstract: A recent work considered the Page curve for entanglement entropy of a freely expanding one-dimensional Fermi gas starting from a finite box (the system) in a zero-temperature initial state that then expands in to a semi-infinite vacuum (the environment). For the case with a single defect at the system-environment junction, it was shown that the Yang-Yang entropy of the system computed from semiclassical hydrodynamics agrees with the microscopically computed entanglement entropy, yielding the Page curve. On the other hand, the environment Yang-Yang entropy showed a monotonic increase. Here, we propose a hydrodynamic description to obtain the eigenvalues of the microscopic correlation matrix for a nonzero temperature freely-expanding Fermi gas. For the system, the phase space density directly gives the correlation matrix eigenvalues and thus, via the Yang-Yang formula, yields the von-Neumann entropy. For the reservoir, a modification of the phase space density is required in the Yang-Yang formula, to incorporate coherences, in order to reproduce accurately the entropy. The hydrodynamic description of correlation matrix eigenvalues also leads to a Levitov-Lesovik type formula for the full-counting-statistics for a finite system in the transient regime. We provide a heuristic derivation of the correlation matrix eigenvalues based on a semiclassical wave-packet picture.
summary: This paper introduces a hydrodynamic framework to determine the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix for an expanding free fermionic gas. By solving the collisionless Boltzmann equation, the authors derive analytic expressions for the system and reservoir entropies. This method successfully reproduces known results for entanglement entropy, providing a semiclassical tool for analyzing non-equilibrium quantum dynamics.
main_problem: The paper develops a hydrodynamic description to calculate the eigenvalues of the microscopic correlation matrix for a free fermionic gas undergoing free expansion at non-zero temperature.
main_result: The hydrodynamic approach successfully predicts the time evolution of the von Neumann entropy and Full Counting Statistics for both the system and the reservoir, showing agreement with exact results for various defect types.
method: The core method involves applying semiclassical hydrodynamics, solving the collisionless Boltzmann equation for the phase space density, and relating the resulting phase space density to the correlation matrix eigenvalues via the Yang-Yang formula.
model_or_system: The system is a one-dimensional free fermionic gas modeled as a finite system coupled to a semi-infinite reservoir via a point defect. The dynamics are governed by the free fermionic Hamiltonian, and the analysis covers different defect types (conformal, hopping, density).
key_observables: Correlation matrix eigenvalues ($\xi_S, \xi_R$), von Neumann entropy ($S_D^{	ext{v}}$), and Full Counting Statistics (FCS).
important_parameters: Temperature ($ eta$), time ($t$), and defect coupling strengths ($g_c$).
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on a semiclassical approximation based on a wave-packet picture, and the leading-order hydrodynamic formula neglects small quantum fluctuations.
figures_summary: Figures compare numerical results against hydrodynamic predictions for eigenvalue profiles, von Neumann entropy, and FCS over time for various defect strengths and temperatures.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the initial problem of calculating correlation matrix eigenvalues to deriving the hydrodynamic equations from the phase space density evolution. It then applies this framework to calculate the entropy for different defect models, comparing the results systematically.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, analytically tractable hydrodynamic tool to study entanglement and thermalization dynamics in open quantum systems, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum information flow in realistic physical settings.
